sections.html:
Madison is the seat of Morgan County, in north central Georgia. Demand for homes here is driven by easy reach of Lake Oconee and four job centers: Atlanta, Athens, Augusta and Macon. Population reached 22,095 by July 2025, a 10.0% gain since April 2020, spread across 9,489 housing units. Roughly 78.2% of those units are lived in by their owners, and the middle home is valued at $342,300.

Madison, Bostwick and Rutledge are cities and Buckhead is a town. Madison adds a city levy to the county one, so a seller inside the city limits settles two bills.

sections.h2: Which two offices handle Morgan County property tax?
sections.html:
Two desks share the work. One sends and collects the bill; the other decides what your house is worth and who gets an exemption.

The Tax Commissioner collects property, mobile home and timber taxes, sells and renews car tags (online renewal is available), and processes title transfers. If you go in person, carry a Georgia license or ID with a Morgan County address.

The Tax Assessor's office is at 150 E Washington Street, Suite 130, Madison, GA 30650. Returns and homestead applications go there, with the return window open January 2 to April 1. A value dispute begins at that counter and can move on to the Board of Equalization, a panel the grand jury appoints.

County commissioners adopt the budget and set the county mill rate. School officials recommend a school rate, and the commissioners almost always have to levy it as recommended. The state's own levy is capped at one fourth of a mill.

sections.h2: Due date and how to pay
sections.html:
Pay by November 15 here. Penalties and interest start after that day. The statewide default is December 20, yet counties may pick December 1 or November 15, and Morgan took the earliest.

Online payment is available through the county's tax payment system. A 60 day grace period runs from the bill's postmark under state rules, so check the bill before counting on a date. The same office collects mobile home and timber tax, so ask the counter for those due dates.

If a sale closes after January 1, settle who pays that year's bill. Whoever owned the house on January 1 is the liable party.

Morgan County layers several exemptions on top of the state basics, and a long-time owner may qualify for more than one. The Tax Assessor decides eligibility.

  • Standard homestead: up to $2,000 is subtracted from assessed value (40% of market value) for county, school and state operating levies.
  • Age 65 and up: a further $10,000 comes off the county and school operating portion, with no income test.
  • Madison residents over 65: another $10,000 off for city maintenance and operations tax.
  • Standard elderly: up to $4,000 off for owners 65 and older when net income, counting a spouse, is $10,000 or less. Social Security and some retirement income do not count toward that limit.
  • Age 65 and older, state portion: the home and up to 10 acres are exempt from the state's levy in full.
  • Disabled veteran rated 100% service connected: a larger deduction that changes every year, with a DD214 and a VA rating letter required.
  • Surviving spouses: an unremarried spouse of a service member killed in war or armed conflict can take up to $50,000, and the unremarried spouse of a firefighter or peace officer killed on duty is fully exempt.

sections.h2: How do I file or keep a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Apply at the Tax Assessor's office. Turn it in whenever you like, though April 1 closes the window for this year and you must have lived in the house on New Year's Day.

Approval is not a yearly chore. Once granted, the exemption rolls forward by itself. A new filing is needed only after a sale, a move, a change to another exemption type, or when income decides eligibility. A denial must be communicated to you by the county, and you may appeal it. Farmland owners can ask the assessor about conservation use, and business owners about personal property.

When a change-of-value notice arrives from the Board of Tax Assessors, 45 days is your window to respond. The assessors review and reply. Still disagree? A Board of Equalization hearing follows, unless you picked arbitration on your original filing.

Before filing, collect a recent appraisal, sale prices of similar homes nearby, and photos of defects that hurt value. Documents persuade better than a feeling that the number is too high.

Three grounds are allowed: taxability, value, and how the value compares with similar properties. Grumbling about the bill itself is not a ground, and a late filing is barred. Superior court stays open after the administrative step. A new return filed during the January 2 to April 1 window can set a different value and protect your appeal rights if the board raises it again.

sections.h2: Other county departments that touch a sale
sections.html:
Planning and Development covers zoning, flood plain management, a fee schedule and the comprehensive plan. Look at the zoning and flood plain pages before listing a lot that sits near water, because buyers and lenders will ask. Roads and Bridges publishes a mowing schedule and a road resurfacing list.

Court Services covers Magistrate Court, Probate Court and Superior Court, which matters if you are selling an inherited house. Solid Waste and Sanitation includes recycling.

Ask the Tax Commissioner for a payoff figure first. If you close before the November 15 bill is due, the closing attorney should spell out who pays it. The state offers no refund for part of a year, so splitting the bill is a contract matter.

A Madison address adds a city bill, so ask which office collects it. Sellers over 65 should check that their exemptions are on the account before the buyer's lender reviews the tax figures. Buyers who will occupy the home file their own application, again by April 1.

Work in this order: get the account balance from the Tax Commissioner, have the Tax Assessor confirm which exemptions are active, then give both to the closing attorney. Doing this early avoids surprises on closing day, since the attorney needs the payoff before preparing the settlement statement.

A cash sale has no lender tax review and no appraisal wait, which can help when a bill is already late. Whatever is owed still comes out of your proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: What is Morgan County's property tax deadline?
faqs.a: November 15, after which penalties and interest build.

faqs.q: Who takes Morgan County homestead applications?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessor, at 150 E Washington Street, Suite 130, in Madison. Aim for April 1 if you want the savings this year.

faqs.q: Can I pay Morgan County property tax online?
faqs.a: Yes, through the county's online tax payment system, which the Tax Commissioner's page links to.

faqs.q: Does Morgan County give seniors an extra exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. Residents 65 and older can take an additional $10,000 off assessed value for county and school maintenance and operations, with no income limit. Madison residents can add the same amount for city tax.

faqs.q: How many days do I have to appeal in Morgan County?
faqs.a: Forty-five, counted from the notice of changed value. The Board of Tax Assessors hears it first.
